corrections.caveats: The printed numbers are the book's own sample run, relayed through the seed lead; they are not on any repo page (the repo carries the benchmark source only, no result files), so they could not be checked against a page. Harness defect visible in the source: opcodes are drawn uniformly from 0 to OP_SENTINEL (6) and OP_HALT is 0, so each of the 2^24 slots is HALT with probability 1/7 and both interpreters return at the first HALT. A timed call therefore runs only a short prefix of the array (about 7 opcodes on average, geometric), the same prefix on every iteration, fully cached and learnable by the branch predictor; it does not exercise a long random dispatch stream as the 2^24 size suggests. The reported 1.41 and 1.82 ns per call amount to only a few clock cycles, consistent with a handful of opcodes, so call overhead and the per-dispatch bounds check weigh heavily in the gap. The prefix also changes between runs because the generator is seeded from std::random_device, so the book's exact workload cannot be reproduced. The switch version carries a default-case range check (needed because enum class op_code can hold any int) that the computed-goto version lacks, so part of the gap is the missing bounds check (a real but documented property of computed-goto dispatch). Computed goto is a GCC/Clang extension; the target is skipped on MSVC. Tier C: first-party book run, compiler, flags and CPU unstated. Only one program per VM, no real bytecode workload, no comparison with a real interpreter such as CPython. The book also notes CPython moved from switch to computed goto in 2008 and to a tail-call interpreter in 2025 (per the lead; not opened). corrections.caveats: The printed numbers are the book's own sample run, relayed through the seed lead; they are not on any repo page (the repo carries the benchmark source only, no result files). The Fibonacci gap is not caused by musttail: the baseline is the exponential-time double recursion while the tail-recursive version is a linear accumulator recursion, so the 2.39 ms versus 6.94 ns gap is an algorithm change, and the tail-recursive version only matches the iterative one (6.94 versus 6.74 ns). The only same-algorithm comparison, factorial, shows the three variants about equal, i.e. no speedup from musttail (an optimizing compiler likely turns the plain accumulator-free factorial recursion into a loop as well). musttail guarantees a jump instead of a call, which matters for stack depth (deep recursion without overflow) rather than speed at these sizes. The musttail macro tests __has_cpp_attribute(clang::musttail) first; GCC 15 implements [[clang::musttail]] (per a WebSearch snippet of the GCC 15.1 release announcement, not opened), so with the repo's GCC 15 Conan profile and with Clang the macro does expand to [[clang::musttail]]; it expands to nothing only on older GCC and MSVC, where the 'musttail' variant is ordinary optimizer-dependent tail recursion. Overflowing uint64_t factorial results are meaningless but harmless to timing; tail_recursion::factorial(0) would not terminate early (checks n == 1 only), irrelevant for the benchmarked n. Category is a best fit only: this is a recursion microbenchmark, not a VM measurement; the technique matters to interpreter design (CPython tail-call interpreter) but nothing here runs a bytecode VM. Tier D: no valid measurement of a speedup from the named technique; the book's run has compiler, flags and CPU unstated. corrections.caveats: The printed numbers are the book's own sample run, relayed through the seed lead; they are not on any repo page (the repo carries the benchmark source only, no result files), so they could not be checked against a page. The comparison is an algorithmic-complexity truism (logarithmic versus linear on sorted data), not a faster implementation of the same algorithm; the speedup grows with n by construction. Both sides are the C++ standard library, so the stdlib under test (libstdc++ per the repo's GCC 15 Conan profile) is not stated for the book's run. Each benchmark repeats the same needle on the same vector, so the about 23 probes of the binary search stay in cache and the 24 ns figure is a warm-cache best case; a random-needle lookup in a 40 MB array would be bound by cache misses. Tier C: first-party book run, compiler, flags and CPU model are unstated (the Google Benchmark context block reports only 20 threads at 2022 MHz, 48 KiB L1d, 24 MiB L3) and the repo holds code only. In the Google Benchmark and Catch2 variants the vector is built outside the timed region; the nanobench_doctest variant builds the vector inside the timed lambda (main_4), so it times construction as well as the search. The same benchmark is written three times (Google Benchmark, Catch2, nanobench with doctest) and only the Google Benchmark numbers are given in the book.
